speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head Q of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Hence, it is critically important that our businesses, both large enterprises as well as small and medium enterprises (SMEs) receive the Government’s support to stay relevant, to innovate and to build deep capabilities to sustain growth right into the future.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Digitalisation is transforming companies, economies and our very way of life.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: A digital economy has many benefits for businesses.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Increased productivity, reduced operating costs and higher asset utilisation are but some of these apparent benefits.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In addition, technology can help us tackle issues, like an ageing population and manpower constraints in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: With declining birth rates, higher life expectancy and more senior citizens opting to remain in the workforce, this ratio is poised to increase over time.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our ageing workforce compels our Large Local Enterprises (LLEs) and SMEs to embrace digitalisation to reap opportunities of the digital economy or risk falling behind.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Across many industries, new technologies are disrupting existing business models.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Leveraging digital platforms, innovative companies have been eroding the market share or even replacing established companies by improving the quality, speed or price at which value is delivered.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: There are numerous examples of such disruptions, ranging from companies disrupted by ride sharing, brick and mortar retail stores disrupted by online 24/7 stores, traditional print media disrupted by social media platforms and so on.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore has done well as we have fast and reliable broadband access and also a high penetration rate for active mobile users.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Even as our businesses aspire to adopt technologies, many companies, especially our SMEs, find it difficult to do so.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: To begin with, SME shareholders and managers often have such questions: "How do I start the digital journey?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Which areas of digitalisation will produce the best returns on investment?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Who can assist me to help fund these investments?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Will it result in near-term losses?" These are but some of the many questions that our SMEs have prior to embarking on the digitalisation journey.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Some key success factors for business digitalisation are scale, large datasets, financial stamina to win market share and to create network effects.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: By definition, SMEs in Singapore are small and our local market is also small.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, the challenges for SMEs to embark on the digitalisation journey are formidable.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our lead enterprises or LLEs also need assistance.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Being larger and operating in more markets, their challenges are less daunting.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our LLEs can then leverage such shared infrastructure to transform their businesses and stay on top of rapid advances in digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our LLEs can then be the receptacle to innovate and be our global champions, leading the way for our SMEs and startups to venture overseas.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Cedric Foo, you can take your next two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Following on my earlier cut on the need for businesses to adopt digital technologies, my next cut is on our workers and measures taken to ensure that we have sufficient talent to support a growing digital economy.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Support for our businesses can be seen as a means to enable our citizens to have good jobs and good wages, thereby improving living standards in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: At the same time, in order for businesses to thrive, they need sufficient workers with digital skills, knowledge and the right attitudes to embrace the constantly evolving digital environment.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This symbiotic relationship is key for a successful digital economy.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: However, many countries, including Singapore, are facing a shortage of workers who are equipped with digital skills necessary for the digital workplace.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: To prepare our youths, basic digital skills and technology literacy have to be introduced at an earlier age.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: They must also be encouraged to challenge the status quo rather than accepting conventional norms, always relooking at how everything is done, thinking expansively on innovative products and solutions.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: More importantly, our workers have to accept that continuous learning is now a norm, and new capabilities and skillsets will have to be acquired many, many times throughout their career life, as the job market would be anything but static.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Over the last few years, the Government has put in place a range of support measures for our workers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Typically, the affected employees, requiring skills retooling, have been loyal employees for years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Upskilling and reskilling these employees will allow the company to retain the organisational values and culture.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Such workers would also have, often times, deep customer relationships that are worth retaining.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: It has always been the case that technological innovation destroys some jobs and replaces them with new ones.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: For many of our workers, especially the older ones, buzz words like "Smart Nation", "digitalisation", "machine learning", artificial intelligence ("AI") and "robotics" can be very disconcerting and intimidating.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: We have to do more to encourage our workers to embrace such changes and reap the tangible benefits of upskilling.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I am thinking that maybe "Natural Language Programming" for oral commands for certain robots, like in the cleaning industry, could be programmed in "Singlish".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Investments in digital talent will be critical to ensuring Singapore remains competitive.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Society will be better off as we invest in our people.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: If ASEAN countries can come together and grow as a single integrated regional digital economy, ASEAN citizens could enjoy significant benefits and improve living standards.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: However, developing a common e-payment system requires close coordination and data flows across boundaries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: But there is a growing number of countries that are enacting laws and barriers that make it more expensive, time-consuming or even illegal to transfer data overseas.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Governments are citing privacy and cybersecurity concerns as they are reluctant to allow a company in another country to have access to their citizens' data.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This is despite the significant economic benefits that we talked about.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Sharing critical information, establishing protocols to deal with hacking, coordinating cyber agencies for ASEAN members and creating a regional dispute settlement resolution are some ways to developing a secure cyberspace.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many companies are still unprepared to go digital in the new world and in the future.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And the Government has been making tremendous and focused efforts to help them go digital, coming up with several schemes and major schemes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, for many companies, due to their business nature and the length of time they have been in business, they are still trying to figure out which part of the process can be digitised.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, it is not just knowing when to start and where to start, there are a couple of scenarios, in my sense, that these businesses cannot see the need to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have been entrenched in the business for too long and they possibly have a winning formula in their business as they have built such depth in their domain knowledge that they did not see the need to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some things are best relied on manual labour, not because it is more cost-effective but because it could possibly give them the efficiency and the margins that they are looking for.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, they do not find the need to change and no motivation to go digital at all.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The business nature and the ecosystem around the business itself creates certain margins that they had for many years.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, status quo helps them to survive and going digital is a form of risk.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, it is the lack of the skill and knowledge within the company, that is, of the bosses, entrepreneurs, founders, staff, workers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is a lot of unwillingness and real intent to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But at the same time, they are reluctant to hire talents or changemakers into a company because that means giving up some of the ownership for those decisions that they have to make.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, how do we get them to digitise?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a sense, are we prepared to allow some of them to consolidate or even fade away if they do not go digital?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are many schemes and programmes rolled out for these local enterprises to help them in this new wave of the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over several weekends, at the grassroots and the community levels, I organised several small gatherings in different locations for residents.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And over time, more and more residents would join such gatherings and we find that it is getting harder and harder to do things in a manual approach, including signing up for some activities or even knowing whether they are going to come or not, as well as conducting surveys with these residents.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We figured that we should digitise the process and then make it a little bit more online that will be more accessible for them and, at the same time, easier to collect the data.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Inclusive of my volunteers and the residents, not everyone is receptive to it.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of course, there are some elderly persons who find it very hard and so we will have to keep the manual process going.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it is an important process to prepare Singaporeans in this digital world because it is not just affecting their daily lives and everything that they do in the near future, but also in finding new jobs or new opportunities in their careers as well as acquiring new skills.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My sense in this process of change is that in preparing Singaporeans to be able to adapt to this new digital world, we certainly still have a distance to go.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, how can Singaporeans be more prepared and what can the Government do to help prepare Singaporeans for this digital age in their daily lives, in finding new jobs, acquiring new skills, so that they could better adapt to this new world?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Automation, digitalisation and AI are disrupting how we live and how work is organised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As old jobs get displaced, new jobs are created that require the right attitude and new competencies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to unlearn and relearn if our people are to exploit the new opportunities and capture value in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it is imperative that we continue to invest in our human capital and help our people transition.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We will also need to accelerate the speed at which we do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government must work with businesses to ensure relevant training content and hands-on practice, culminating in real job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am aware of the Infocomm Media Development Authority's (IMDA's) effort in running human capital programmes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Do the new jobs and skills trained match well?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If there are, what is the success rate so far?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Douglas Foo, you can take your two next cuts together.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, on SMEs Go Digital, since the launch of the SMEs Go Digital programme during Budget 2017, the programme has helped and has developed many initiatives with the aim of helping local SMEs use digital technologies, build capabilities and participate in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Through partnerships with trade associations and chambers (TACs), such as the Singapore Manufacturing Federation, the programme provides SMEs with consultancy advice from specialist digital project managers to help them implement pre-approved digital solutions to transform their businesses.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, can the Ministry provide a progress update on the SMEs Go Digital programme, particularly with respect to the minimum number of SMEs the programme is intended to reach, and how the Ministry intends to get SMEs to accelerate the adoption of digital solutions?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the manufacturing sector advances towards Industry 4.0, the sector will increasingly require the skillset of info-communications media (ICM) professionals to harness frontier technologies to help the sector reach Industry 4.0's standards sooner.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the ITM's employment goals so far?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what are the Ministry of Communications and Information's (MCI's) long-term plans to attract talents to become ICM professionals?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: People assume that your services will always be available whenever they want it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They give no thought to the effort and planning that go into providing such services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the moment there is any disruption, everybody is instantly up in arms.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, consumers were outraged by a 3.5 hours' outage in Singtel's broadband services in July last year, or another similar disruption in November.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The digital economy – streaming services, e-commerce, cloud computing – is built on the assumption of uninterrupted access to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But no matter how much service providers invest to ensure 99.999% uptime, it can be undone by failure at the infrastructure level.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Loss of connectivity can have potentially catastrophic business consequences as businesses are unable to access customers or essential services, such as banking, payments and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Concepts that seemed like science fiction just a few years ago are starting to impact our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Autonomous vehicles, intelligent home automation, bots powered by natural language processing that can hold an almost human-like conversation, these things are already here.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The impact that they will have on our daily lives is still not fully understood, but will surely be profound.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It will shape how we live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has invested billions of dollars to support research into such areas.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The current Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE 2020) plan has allocated $19 billion to key areas, such as advanced manufacturing and urban solutions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the SingHealth cyberattack was the largest breach in Singapore to date.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, there does not appear to be any remedy or compensation available to the actual victims of the data breach.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There is no obvious recourse for the ones who had their personal data stolen.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to fines, can we provide a way for victims of data breaches to claim compensation for the loss of personal data?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In December 2017, Uber delayed in reporting that personal information of 380,000 users in Singapore had been compromised in a breach the year before.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: After the breach had occurred and before Uber's admission of the said breach, it was reported that victims of the data breach were preyed upon by the hackers who used the stolen personal data to cause even more harm to the victims.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is unclear how many of those victims suffered further losses as a result of the actions of the hackers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible to have a tribunal to allow the victims to seek compensation for any losses they might have suffered as a result of the data breach?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, the PDPC was set up in 2013 as the implementing agency for the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister recently pointed out that in the SingHealth data breach, the PDPC had leveraged the findings of a Committee of Inquiry (COI) called by the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If another major breach were to occur and a COI is not formed, does PDPC have the resources to investigate a major case on its own?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to ask about outcomes achieved for complainants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where the PDPC found that organisations were in breach of their obligations to safeguard personal data, it was usual that PDPC will impose financial penalties and also give directions on how the organisations should improve its data security arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This exclusion seems artificial when data is collected by entities under PDPA obligations and then transmitted to the Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, during the Committee of Supply (COS) debate last week on the Smart Nation topic, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan mentioned that Singapore was going to "double down" on AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He pointed out that AI, and in particular, deep machine learning, has revolutionised many services, including providing voice assistants, language translations, global positioning system optimisation and helping to detect fraud.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are revolutionary developments and Singapore must continue down this path.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, there are concerns about AI being used improperly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Machines, like humans, need to be taught and trained, and this requires access to data.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have some concerns that people may not be aware of the full extent to which their personal data is being gathered and used.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second, of course, is after this data is gathered and technology is developed, the same information in the wrong hands can lead to trouble, including in the hands of foreign actors, hackers and scammers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, as we make definitive strides in realising our Smart Nation ambitions, I greatly welcome the announcement of the Proposed Model AI Governance Framework.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: While big data, deep learning and neural networks may sound abstract, their growing deployment has real consequences for society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: AI-driven automated decision-making is increasingly being used for systems and processes that determine product prices, insurance premiums and job recruitment, just to name a few.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These are areas where alarms about algorithmic bias have, indeed, been raised.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Issues relating to data justice, algorithmic fairness and explainable AI must thus be closely monitored to ensure that we reap the best of technology while effectively managing unintended adverse consequences.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The Proposed Model AI Governance Framework is, therefore, especially timely.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It will help to warrant that our drive for innovation does not leave ethicality in the dust.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: By enunciating a common AI governance approach and offering a set of consistent definitions and principles relating to the responsible use of AI, we provide greater certainty to industry players.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Can MCI, therefore, share its plans for ensuring that this framework is effectively disseminated across all relevant industries?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How will it raise awareness of the guidelines governing the responsible use of AI and encourage their application?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Are there also plans to have this framework introduced into the curriculum of students taking AI-related courses in our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs)?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I understand that the Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) sectors have been established with the express aim of improving cybersecurity so as to ensure the continuous delivery of essential services in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I applaud the Government's efforts at safeguarding our digital sphere.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is of paramount importance as we make the transition into a Smart Nation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Recent events, both domestically and internationally, such as the cyberattacks on SingHealth and the recent hack into the Australian parliament's computer network, underscore the threats that we face, and the necessity for swift, decisive action to mitigate or neutralise these threats.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having said this, I would like to seek some clarification in three areas: first, what are the essential public services that have been identified under the CII?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, how will the infrastructure pertaining to these sectors be set up or otherwise modified to ensure robust cybersecurity?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Third, what are the contingencies that the Government will employ in the event of a cyberattack or disruption of essential services?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: Recently, I had a chat at the workspace in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: The workspace is occupied by many entrepreneurs and many of them build their business using the Internet or social media as a platform.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: So, I had a chat with this user.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: He runs an e-commerce company and he told me that one day, he woke up and he realised that there was no sale within his system.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: He was wondering why and, actually, his system was hacked.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: His customer database was hacked, as well as the entire website was hacked.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: What happened was he had to close the business for a few days and he almost had to close the entire business.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck
text: If we could, we should educate more and more businesses, especially the smaller businesses and the startups which are building their businesses over the Internet, about cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is appropriate, coming after the SingHealth attack and the HIV Registry leak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is one critical vulnerability that now needs addressing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) has also been relying on private companies to drive technological innovation and adaptations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been suggested that the Government should provide grants for SMEs to train employees and improve cyber defences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, it has also been suggested that a Government hotline be established for businesses to obtain advice and report cybersecurity breaches without adversarial treatment from the Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Mr Chairman, as more and more of our systems go online, cybersecurity becomes a particular concern.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The two high-profile incidents this year highlight our vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This highlighted that there are well-funded organisations and countries out there that may deliberately try and break into our systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This highlighted that a human lapse by one of the individuals entrusted with access to the system, coupled with malicious intent by another, can lead to disastrous consequences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These incidents show two aspects of the vulnerability of our Government systems, and it is foreseeable that both of these, external threats as well as human error by trusted individuals, are timeless issues that are almost impossible to eradicate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Against this backdrop, are there ways to assess the cybersecurity of our Government systems and better improve it?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, according to the Global Cybersecurity Index 2017, Singapore topped the list as the country that was prepared against cyberattacks, surpassing the United States (US).

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: However, despite the robustness of our cybersecurity strategy, attacks, such as the one on MOH, demands that we continue to be vigilant and steadfast in our defence against cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Just like the other pillars of Total Defence, Digital Defence involves everyone, from individuals to businesses to the Government.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Therefore, can the Ministry explain how it intends to encourage collaboration amongst industry partners to harness local cybersecurity expertise to develop secure, high-quality products that contribute towards a safe and trusted cyberspace for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The advent of technology has brought with it new ecosystems and new methods of engagement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Technology and, in particular, the Internet, has changed the way we socialise, work and do business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These changes have brought about massive improvements by connecting people as well as increasing efficiency and productivity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there are people who have sought to misuse and cause harm to others on these new platforms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Private entities are also prime targets for digital attacks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In 2017, Uber announced that the personal information of over 57 million Uber users and 600,000 drivers were exposed by hackers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In November 2018, Marriot International also announced that cybercriminals stole data of approximately 500 million customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As the Government boosts the nation's cybersecurity infrastructure and strengthens the legal framework to deal with digital crime, it is important for the community to be equipped with sufficient knowledge and skills to protect themselves from online harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Individual users, businesses and organisations need to be prepared.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The most robust cyber defences are susceptible to breaches even by the act of that one single user, whether it is because of lax passwords, unknowingly leaking confidential data or falling prey to phishing attacks that trick users into giving up sensitive data.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, how can we improve cybersecurity awareness among citizens and businesses so that we can continue to leverage the opportunities that technology brings while minimising the threats online?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Manpower planning and talent development strategy are critical in the national strategy to strengthen cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 2012, the Economic Development Board (EDB) reported that there were 1,200 cybersecurity specialists although there are 140,000 information technology (IT) professionals.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: After seven years, where do we stand today in terms of number and percentage of cybersecurity specialists among IT professionals?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How many more are needed and being targeted?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: One of the key thrusts of the National Cyber Security Masterplan 2018 is to grow Singapore's expertise in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Infocomm Development Authority (IDA) has been working with our IHLs to expand cybersecurity programmes.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Polytechnics and industry have collaborated to establish cybersecurity centres.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: IDA is also collaborating with FireEye to upskill cybersecurity professionals.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: EDB and NEC corporation are collaborating to develop capabilities in strategic areas through overseas attachment.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: ST Engineering established the DigiSAFE Cyber Security Centre to reskill those interested in a mid-career switch.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: With the establishment of the Home Team Science and Technology Agency and MINDEF’s Defence Cyber Organisation, and also the public sector Cybersecurity Professional Programme and MINDEF's Cyber Full-time National Servicemen (NSF) Vocation, we now have a varied landscape for manpower and talent development in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Are these different efforts being coordinated by the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) and IDA in accordance with the national strategy?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Are these efforts competing with one another for a small pool of talents or complementing one another for synergies?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, the anonymous nature of the Internet has led to a "disinhibition effect" where people take on an online persona that is different from their persona in real life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The disinhibition effect has been studied extensively by researchers to understand cyberbullying behaviour and other forms of undesirable online behaviour, such as trolling and catfishing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While such online behaviour is objectionable, its effect is relatively contained.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is worrying is the emergence of deliberate online falsehoods, where the reach and potential impact of such falsehoods are widespread.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Internet has provided the perpetrators of falsehoods with a veil of anonymity and the disinhibition effect has emboldened the perpetrators to craft messages that are patently false, with the malicious intention to obfuscate the truth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The malice of online falsehood can lead to communal and racial violence, distrust in the establishment and sway public opinions on important social issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is not immune to the malice of deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some state actors and individuals have mounted falsehood campaigns to discredit our institutions, to cast aspersions on our Government and systems.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These orchestrated campaigns need to be dealt with swiftly and decisively before they gain momentum.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, dealing with deliberate online falsehoods require a multi-agency approach that includes combating falsehoods with facts, educating Singaporeans to discern between truth and untruth, and for media companies to play their part to weed out fake posts and misinformation campaigns.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some concrete steps that the Government is taking to help Singaporeans guard against deliberate online falsehoods in an increasingly complex digital and media environment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, this House set up a Select Committee to look into the matter of Deliberate Online Falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I should declare that I participated in the public consultation by the Select Committee as part of the People's Action Party (PAP) Policy Forum.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: Mr Chairman, I commend the establishment of the Digital Readiness Blueprint but would like to ask how it caters to the varying skillsets of Internet users.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: While we, fortunately, do not have a digital access divide in Singapore, research around the world has shown that the "second level digital divide" pertaining to online skills can significantly influence how much people can benefit from their online experience.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: Furthermore, with our high smartphone penetration rates, we need to pay particular attention to Internet use via mobile phones.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: Because the mobile Internet is centred around apps, mobile-only users who rely exclusively on mobile devices are quite distinct from mobile-first users who use mobile devices predominantly but in combination with other devices.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: These differing usage patterns can translate into different online experiences that reflect variances in online competencies and breadth of exposure to content.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: These can, in turn, shape individual worldviews and understanding of key societal issues that impact their personal lives.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Mr Chairman, there are several reasons for the digital divide.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: The primary one is a lack of ready access to computers, smartphones and the Internet.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: To be applauded are initiatives, such as Home Access programmes for low-income families and Enable IT for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Both these programmes have done well to provide affordable and inclusive digital access for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Another reason for the digital divide is the lack of skills, as Prof Lim Sun Sun pointed out just now, to use digital technologies safely and confidently.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Besides being able to operate a device, it is also important for good cyber hygiene habits, including awareness of the negative impact of technology, such as fake news, cyberbullying and social isolation.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Yet another reason for the digital divide is the lack of willingness of some of our citizens to participate in a digital economy.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: High-profile cyberattacks, including the SingHealth data breach last year, have some of our citizens fearing the use of digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Yet others have been deterred when they hear of people falling victim to online scams.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Chairman, digital services have become an increasingly central part of our lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We all use mobile apps multiple times each day.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: From games to health tracking to stock market information, we hardly even notice them anymore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: They have become so fundamental to our lives that the United Nations (UN) has even spoken of protecting Internet access as a key element of protecting an individual’s rights.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: However, there is also increasing concern about a "digital divide".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Lower-income groups are going to be disadvantaged if they lack exposure to the digital world due to affordability concerns.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Apart from lack of access to more affordable substitutes for physical services, they may also fail to acquire essential skills needed to work productively in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: If children from lower-income households miss out on digital experiences, we risk creating a permanent underclass.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Significant steps have already been made to address this issue, such as the Home Access Programme, which provides eligible households with two years of subsidised fibre broadband.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Free WiFi hotspots are also becoming increasingly common.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: What more can we do to ensure that digital connectivity is affordable for the vulnerable and disadvantaged segments of our society?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Chairman, as we gear up for a digital economy, we must make sure that our people are able to benefit from this transformation and not be left behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must not inadvertently create a new inequality or widen an existing gap between those who can access and exploit the new digital technologies and those who cannot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Whilst future generations of elderly will be better-educated and tech-savvy, we must not neglect our current generation of seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need Smart Seniors for a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need to harness technology to supplement our shortage of eldercare manpower and help more seniors live independently in the comfort of their own homes and community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We need to harness technology to help them stay connected to news and information, support networks, friends and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: To do all these, it is important to ensure that they are digitally ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Digital readiness is the very first step and a critical enabler for our elderly to fully exploit the benefits of technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, my grassroots team and I actively seek out partners with the resources to help our seniors and digitally vulnerable residents to overcome these barriers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: This is done mainly through SkillsFuture @ Libraries workshops held in our libraries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Also, I would like to seek an update as to how the Ministry has encouraged adult learners to use library resources.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: This information can be subsequently used in the recommendation of library resources, such as books, e-books, audiobooks and videos, to users to aid in their self-development and learning.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: This data-sharing platform will collate information, such as the career aspirations, sector of work or interests, of users who have registered with SkillsFuture.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Subsequently, knowledge, resources and skills which are of interest or are beneficial to the respective users can be identified.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: The relevant resources can then be recommended to users through the NLB mobile app.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: This will allow users to identify the materials which will best aid in their self-improvement and learning and encourage self-learning.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: In essence, this approach will allow for the customisation of tailor-made learning programmes suited to the individual learning needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: These learning pods contain video tutorials on various subjects ranging from coding to business.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: We should encourage the proliferation of these learning pods throughout libraries across Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: I urge the Ministry to expedite the development of our libraries into self-learning hubs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, can you take one cut?

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are going for tea break after this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Libraries today face critical challenges from many counts: from the Internet, modern cafes and even homes with book repositories.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The question is not whether print and digital media can exist side by side in libraries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: It is how the library can be a third space, for diverse social groups to exchange ideas, inclusively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Libraries can be physical or virtual social spaces with social media applications.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: How can we transform our libraries into community hubs for people to interact, interconnect, learn, produce, share, meet informally, hold discussions or organise social events, special shows and exhibitions?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Libraries can also be "living rooms" for sharing of ideas via book clubs and forums, a safe space and meeting place for all.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.57 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to speak on civic discussions and diversity of views.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Global cities across the world are often characterised by openness and tolerance of divergent views.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: One significant trait of such vibrant societies is the people's ability to "talk" through multiple, conflicting perspectives without hysteria and harm.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While psychologists argue that it is social survival depends on conformity, recent research also suggests that divergence fosters creativity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Stanford Professor Carol Dweck has done extensive work on the concept of "Growth Mindset." Individuals who believe their talents can be developed through hard work, good strategies and input from others have this growth mindset.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I believe that respect for divergent views can be fostered in our schools to help students engage calmly in rational exchange to develop a growth mindset.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I would like the Government to consider how we can we improve civic discussion in our schools and beyond to encourage the plurality of views among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, before I begin, I declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer of a research consultancy that undertakes surveys.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, charities could design better fundraising programmes to help their beneficiaries by understanding the climate of public opinion around the issues and beneficiaries they are addressing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academics could mine such surveys for research purposes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Civil society groups could use survey data to develop better programmes to raise awareness around their focused issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Citizens could use that knowledge to better shape and calibrate their actions as citizens, for example, in writing letters to the media, expressing views on social media and making representations to consultative committees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The results of those surveys should be available for all to use, not only the Government and Government leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Well-meaning policies can become ineffective and rile people if communications are not done well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Worse, in the absence of effective policy communications, those who wish us ill could exploit the opportunity to distort facts or spread fake news.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It would be tragic if policies designed with Singapore's and Singaporeans' best interest in mind are misunderstood and fail to receive public support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Conversely, policies that are effectively communicated can receive widespread public support, thereby ensuring their successful implementation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Mother tongue and National Service policies are excellent examples.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We can observe the robust public support these policies receive till this day because people understood the rationale, despite the personal sacrifices they may have to make.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Effective policy communications, therefore, strengthen our national solidarity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, please take the next two cuts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, first, is on public service broadcasting (PSB).

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Over the years, IMDA has supported the production of PSB programmes which have several national and social objectives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: PSB programmes promote Singapore, the Singapore identity and values, such as family, community, social inclusiveness and cohesiveness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: At the same time, they cater to special interest groups, for example, the elderly and youths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: They have also helped to increase cultural awareness in a plural society and foster religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Over the years, such programmes have also helped to educate viewers, for example, through current affairs exposure so that we can be plugged into the world as global citizens to understand the cross currents that affect us.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Today, a revolution called cord-cutting is spreading throughout the world, freeing people from the ties to cable even, with over-the-top (OTT) services offered by Netflix, Amazon Prime and even Viu for fans who want to binge-watch Korean content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: In the last five years, efforts to grow the media industry has rapidly accelerated.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Big players like Lucasfilm; RGM Holdings, a well-known talent management company; BKN Media, an acclaimed animation studio; and DLM Digital Studios, a major Indian film production company, have set up shop in Singapore, increasing the international profile of the media industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: In the area of media education, Nanyang Technological University's (NTU's) School of Arts Design and Media has launched programmes to nurture creative media professionals.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: South Seas Film and Television School from New Zealand is also setting up a campus here.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This will provide many opportunities for classrooms to become media hubs for media talent in the making.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: However, it has been observed that the local market for made-in-Singapore media content is small, making it imperative to create an enabling media environment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, may I first seek your permission to display some slides in the course of my speech?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In my response, I would outline MCI's plans to secure Singapore's future in a digital age, as part of the Ministry's broader mission to connect our people to opportunities, communities and the Government.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will address cybersecurity and digital readiness, while	Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will do so for the media sector and Government communications.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I will conclude with our plans for the libraries and archives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Every enterprise, regardless of size or stage of development, can use technology to innovate and grow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Every worker, regardless of industry or education level, can use technology to be more effective and productive.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And every citizen, regardless of age or background, can use technology confidently and enrich their lives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This vision is already being realised, sometimes in quite unlikely quarters of our economy and society.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Small enterprises in traditional sectors are harnessing technologies to grow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I recently met Mr Selvam, he was a former commando, who now owns Anushia Flower Shop in Little India, a testament to the diverse capabilities of our Singapore Armed Forces officers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He has used e-commerce to reach corporate clients and new customers, to increase his revenue by 50%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the opening of library@harbourfront in January, I saw seniors effortlessly reading e-newspapers and learning enthusiastically to use the different apps on their smartphones.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Children were enjoying themselves in the Immersive Storytelling Room and adults were using the NLB Mobile App.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to build on this momentum by nurturing a vibrant ICM industry, comprising businesses with deep capabilities, workers who are highly skilled and a world-class digital infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We start with efforts to raise the digital capabilities of our broad base of enterprises, especially our SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Cedric Foo and Mr Douglas Foo have asked how we are helping businesses benefit from digital technologies, and Mr Teo Ser Luck asked about the outcomes of our efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Two years ago, we launched the SMEs Go Digital programme and the results have been encouraging.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Proven digital solutions are provided, and consultancy and project management services are also available.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have been adapting the SMEs Go Digital programme to the changing needs of businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This way, businesses benefit from the very beginning, and they can also build on these digital foundations as they scale.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also expanding the SMEs Go Digital to meet the more complex needs of businesses as they scale.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Rhyce and Gary Chng are brothers who own this local logistics and transportation company.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And they are now extending the platform to fellow SMEs as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Beyond the enterprises, we have also embarked on digital initiatives at the systems-level so that we can derive broader benefits.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The nationwide e-invoicing network is one such initiative which IMDA launched in January this year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Invoicing is a key business function, but manual processes can be tedious and error-prone.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With e-invoicing, businesses can streamline processes, increase accuracy and improve cash flow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government, on its part, is fully committed to this initiative and will prepare our system to receive e-invoices by this year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I want to encourage all our businesses to use this nationwide network to improve their efficiency and reduce their costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Another example is a system-level initiative is TradeTrust, which aims to streamline and digitalise our trade processes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A common challenge in the trade and logistics sectors is the inefficiency of manual cross-border trade processes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: TradeTrust is an initiative to develop a set of standards to help businesses securely exchange digital trade documents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will enhance our attractiveness as a business hub and improve the efficiency of our trading and logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IMDA and other Government agencies are now working with industry partners to conduct proof-of-concept trials, and we will provide more details later.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The digitalisation of our businesses can succeed only if our workers, too, are equipped to effectively use digital technology.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many Members – Mr Cedric Foo, Mr Teo Ser Luck, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Douglas Foo – have asked how we are preparing workers and growing our talent for the digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I agree with Mr Teo Ser Luck it is a challenge.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a challenge, both of changing mindsets and developing the will to make the change happen.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In 2016, we launched the TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA) programme to meet the growing demand for digitally-skilled professionals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These courses provide opportunities for non-ICT workers to switch into a tech career, as well as for current ICT workers to take on deeper tech roles.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Xie Zhaoyan is one of our graduates from TeSA's Tech Immersion and Placement Programme, which helps non-ICT workers move into the field.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through the programme, he acquired software development skills which helped him make the transition from being an engineer in the oil and gas industry, to a data engineer at Amaris AI where he develops applications for clients.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: TeSA also has a Company Led Training (CLT) programme where, as the name suggests, companies take the lead to train ICT workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I recently visited Tunity Technologies, a local radio frequency identification (RFID) solutions provider.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The SME has helped train and hire six workers through the programme, including Ms Yeo Wan Ru.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many of them also stay with the same company they were placed in.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We also conduct periodic reviews and work closely with key hirers of ICT professionals to assess the outcomes of our programmes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Tech companies, like Tunity, play an important role in the training and growth of our ICT workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through our local partners, Kaplan and Trent Global, we will also create more upskilling opportunities for our workers by bringing in renowned training curriculum by METIS for data science from the US, and Code Institute for software development from Ireland.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These will help more workers and companies seize opportunities arising from the digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And as every worker has different digital training needs, we will also roll out the Digital Learning Guide.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will enable employers to plan for their workers' digital training needs using a step-by-step guide.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will start with the retail and logistics sectors and progressively extend it to others.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We also want to harness the talent of the many Singaporeans who are working overseas in key tech areas and who are eager to contribute to Singapore's digital transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To encourage such tech talent flows, I am pleased to inform Members of the launch of the Overseas Singaporeans in Tech (OST)-LinkedIn community, which is a partnership between the industry and key Government agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will connect overseas Singaporean tech talent with our local tech community and keep them informed of the latest developments back home.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Since the group was formed in January this year, it has managed to get in touch with over 500 Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Investment in research and development (R&D) is also an essential part of our efforts to help industries innovate and stay competitive, even as the technology landscape is rapidly evolving.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our R&D investments in the Services and Digital Economy (SDE) domain of the RIE2020 Plan have helped us build capabilities in frontier tech areas and address our national priorities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, through AI Singapore's Grand Challenges, we are working with academia and industry to solve major problems faced in the key sectors, such as healthcare.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This increase is part of the next phase of the National Research Foundation's RIE2020 plan, which will be announced soon.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also establishing Digital Services Labs to unlock value from our R&D investments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This programme will work with technology providers, research and industry partners to co-develop cutting-edge technology to address business challenges.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Effective regulations that keep abreast of change and innovation and world-class digital infrastructure underpin our Digital Economy vision.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In that regard, we are reviewing our Electronic Transactions Act to cater for new business models, new technologies and national projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also reviewing PDPA so that it continues to safeguard consumer interests while enabling the innovative use of data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PDPC has the expertise and resources to investigate different types of data protection breaches and, where necessary, works with external parties on investigations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because it is cited within IMDA, the agency is also able to ride on IMDA's broader infrastructure and overheads and focus its resources on investigations and some of the core areas of work.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will continue to ensure that PDPC is adequately resourced and fit-for-purpose.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I had also explained in Parliament on 12 February why public agencies are not covered by PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to inform Ms Sylvia Lim that the reasons have not changed in the next past weeks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are covered not only by PSGA but also other specific legislation and the Government Instruction Manual, which Ms Sylvia Lim has also acknowledged.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When necessary, PDPC helps to link individuals with the organisation and its data protection officers to address specific data protection concerns that have been raised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad asked about recourse available for individuals affected by data breaches.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Individuals who suffer loss can seek legal advice on available recourse, including seeking compensation directly from the organisation or by taking private action against the organisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Individuals may also resolve data protection disputes through mediation by the Consumers Association of Singapore or the Singapore Mediation Centre.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also preparing for new technologies like AI.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have also established an Advisory Council on the Ethical Use of AI and Data and launched a research programme to advance discourse on legal and ethical AI issues.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun will be happy to note that we are engaging partners like the Advisory Council, sector regulators and TACs to promote the adoption of the Framework.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our efforts in AI governance and ethics have also received international recognition as a World Summit on the Information Society Prizes 2019 Champion.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, this is an acknowledgment at an international fora of the work that we are doing, but we are pressing ahead because the landscape is evolving.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And 5G has the potential to fundamentally transform our businesses and the way they operate, given its capacity to handle many high-demand applications simultaneously, such as the connectivity of autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, the deployment of IoT and nationwide sensor networks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Cedric Foo's point, we are strong advocates for open cross-border data flows, which is essential if we are to fully harness the potential of technologies like AI.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the regional level, we have helped set baseline data protection principles in the region by contributing to the ASEAN Framework on Digital Data Governance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We also participate in multilateral certification mechanisms like the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Cross-Border Privacy Rules and Privacy Recognition for Processors systems.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have included commitments to promote data flows in free trade agreements, such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, collectively, these initiatives will enable businesses to transfer data across borders seamlessly and securely and seize new digital opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But these opportunities can only be meaningfully realised within a safe and secure cyberspace.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I agree with Mr Teo Ser Luck and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh that besides helping SMEs benefit from digitalisation, we must help them protect their businesses from cyber threats.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, CSA and IMDA will expand the range of pre-approved solutions to include cybersecurity solutions later this year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This will give SMEs some guidance into the kind of solutions they can adopt and strengthen their cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin asked how we are protecting our CIIs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It empowers CSA to effectively combat cyberattacks and investigate cyber incidents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: All CIIs have been designated by the end of 2018.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our 11 CII sectors provide essential services, such as transport, energy and water supply, and all CII owners must adhere to the Cybersecurity Code of Practice.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Regular penetration tests are also conducted to identify and rectify vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, we have in place measures to enhance resilience, including contingency and incident response plans in the event that a cyberattack causes the disruption of essential services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We launched Digital Defence as the sixth pillar of Total Defence last month.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It was in recognition of the fact that each and every citizen, business and organisation has a role to play in helping us develop robust defences against threats from cyberspace.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To paraphrase the old saying, we are only as strong as the weakest cyber link.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will be sharing more details on our cybersecurity efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Building digital readiness is a national effort involving the Government, businesses, communities and individuals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is why we are launching the Digital Participation Pledge which allows organisations to commit to one or more actionable items that help Singaporeans acquire skills and adopt technology.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So far, more than 270 organisations have pledged to do their part, and we hope to see more organisations sign up so that, together, we can build a more digitally ready Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am heartened by the many volunteers and corporate partners who have come forward to volunteer at our Digital Clinics to assist citizens in using mobile devices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Standard Chartered Bank is a corporate partner with more than 200 of their staff members volunteering.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One of the volunteers, Ms Audrey Poh, shared with me that she was inspired by the participants' enthusiasm to learn as she taught them to use different apps.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken at length on our broad range of efforts to help our enterprises and people benefit from the opportunities presented by the digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is not an easy task nor is it the sole responsibility of the Government.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, ultimately, every business, every worker and every citizen has to step up, overcome the challenges, and take ownership of their learning and digital transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Chairman, if I may have your permission to show this video which aptly captures the challenge that we are dealing with?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is what my younger colleagues in the Ministry called a "bold" or "edgy" video.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Chairman, as technology becomes part of our lives, we need to strengthen our digital readiness and our cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We must ensure that all Singaporeans have access to the tools and knowledge to benefit from technology, and that workers and businesses will thrive in a cybersecure environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Several Members have expressed concerns about segments of our society that may be slower or less likely to benefit from the digital transformation journey that Singapore is undergoing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We must ensure that the benefits of digitalisation are enjoyed by all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It requires the combined efforts of the Government, businesses and the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This Council will provide strategic direction, guide the implementation of our digital readiness initiatives, and examine the needs of the community in terms of digital inclusion, literacy and participation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Importantly, and very hearteningly, as Minister noted, we have received significant support from the wider community and businesses to serve on the Council and its working committees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our efforts can be categorised into these three areas: digital participation, digital inclusion and digital literacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For Digital Participation, we will launch two new initiatives to mobilise organisations from the private, people and public sectors to drive our digital readiness efforts and bring more citizens on board the digital readiness movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In another realm – also for digital participation but focusing on the community – we have partnered MCCY to create Our Singapore Fund for Digital Readiness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This encourages community efforts to promote digital readiness and enlarge the social commons by the non-profit sector around digital readiness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Moving on to Digital Inclusion, and to answer Mr Cedric Foo, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Rahayu Mahzam about how we are helping everyone benefit from technology, digital inclusion requires access to technology, as well as the skills and knowledge to use it safely and confidently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have organised over 90 Digital Clinics since 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These Digital Clinics were by appointment, or irregular, ad hoc and often organised together with events.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To provide this as a permanent service to residents, we launched the Tech Connect service, starting at eight community centres last November.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This service provides residents with personal assistance in a language they are comfortable with on how to use digital devices and applications like Facebook and WhatsApp, so that they can connect with friends and family, build stronger social networks and use technology in everyday aspects of their lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They can also seek help for very practical issues, like how to reset a password.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This service will be rolled out to all community centres progressively as a permanent service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are encouraged by the large number of seniors who have picked up basic digital skills through our Silver Infocomm Initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To Mr Ong Teng Koon's query on how we are ensuring that digital connectivity remains affordable, the Home Access Programme and the NEU PC Plus programme provide subsidised infocomm devices and Internet access to low-income households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To date, more than 70,000 households have benefited from these programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These sort of programmes have existed as public sector programmes since 1999 for more than 20 years trying to find ways to make sure that vulnerable, lower-income households that will benefit from that type of connectivity will have access to connectivity, as well as the devices to make use of that connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have different programmes, depending on whether there are school-going children in the household.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, MCI is working with IMDA and the People's Association (PA) to run a pilot programme for elderly residents in MacPherson and Radin Mas constituencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We plan to provide 200 residents who do not have mobile devices or Internet connectivity with data-equipped smartphones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Grassroots volunteers will provide guidance to help residents build skills and confidence in using this technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is part of a study – an experiment, a pilot – to find out how we can encourage and support the adoption of digital technology, among the digitally less ready.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun has asked how we can help individuals acquire the necessary skills, and ascertain what competencies are needed to function effectively in the digital economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Her questions address the third component of digital readiness, after Participation and Inclusion, which is Digital Literacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: IMDA has developed a Basic Digital Skills Curriculum to ensure that citizens can pick up these skills in a structured manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The skills identified in the curriculum correspond to everyday activities, with an emphasis on prevailing technology trends, such as the use of e-payments and mobile applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The curriculum is being offered as a one-day course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Those who are keen to pick up Basic Digital Skills at their own pace can also do so online at the IM Silver portal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will periodically refresh the curriculum and curate relevant content for seniors, taking into account emerging trends and feedback from stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Darryl David and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked how Singaporeans can navigate an increasingly complex cyberspace and given the threat of deliberate online falsehoods, cybercrime and cyberattacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Technology offers us greater convenience and greater connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But it can be stressful to navigate the complex web of websites, applications and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Online threats worsen anxiety, reduce trust and undermine public confidence in institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have seen this happen in other countries, and Singapore is not immune.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A well-informed and discerning public is Singapore’s first and most important line of defence against online threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Government is improving public education to tackle the serious and pervasive problem of deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Evaluate" (SURE) programme, raises awareness of the dangers and how to discern fake news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Ministry of Education's (MOE’s) New Media Literacies toolkit supports teachers’ efforts to help students navigate the digital environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This includes learning how to detect falsehoods on social media, and how to interact responsibly with others online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
